# What a System of Record Is

A system of record is not a better document. It is a document that other copies defer to.

## Three properties

**Authority.** When two versions disagree, one of them wins by definition. Without that rule you
have two documents and an argument.

**Provenance.** Every claim can be traced to the source it came from, with its numbers and
qualifiers intact. "Up to $500,000" never softens into "about $500,000" on the way in.

**Abstention.** The corpus is finite on purpose, so "that is not covered here" is a correct answer.
An assistant that fills the gap from general knowledge destroys the guarantee the corpus exists to
provide — the reader can no longer tell which sentences were checked.

:::warning[A citation is not a warranty]

Provenance proves who said something and when. It does not prove the claim is still true.

:::

## What it is not

Provenance proves who said something and when. It does **not** prove the claim is right, current,
or uncontested. A correct answer from 2019 is a wrong answer now, and no citation can tell the
difference — which is why an effective date belongs in the document itself.

## The governance ladder

Governance arrives in rungs, not all at once. A corpus at level 0 already works: documents in, two
surfaces out. Higher rungs add review records, approval, and the ability to prove who authorised
what — and a project climbs only as far as its domain actually requires.

```text
level 0   documents compile and serve
level 1   sources and effective dates recorded
level 2   review recorded against each document
level 3   approval, with an accountable owner
level 4   audit: every served answer replayable
```

Demanding level 4 of a level-0 project is a bug, not rigour.
